title: Statute of Frauds (Title 32, Chapter 3)
date_or_version: Current unannotated Code as shown on page
legal_subject: Contract enforceability: which agreements must be in writing
verification_status: Verified: page text read directly on scstatehouse.gov
what_it_says_and_notes: No action may be brought on five listed categories of agreement (including an agreement not to be performed within one year, and promises to answer for another's debt) unless the agreement or a memorandum of it is in writing and signed by the party to be charged. Site discloses the unannotated Code is not the official version.

title: Limitation of Civil Actions, general contract periods (Title 15, Chapter 3)
date_or_version: Current unannotated Code as shown on page
legal_subject: Breach of contract: time limit to sue
verification_status: Verified: page text read directly on scstatehouse.gov (via the no-www address of the same page)
what_it_says_and_notes: § 15-3-530(1): three years for an action on a contract, obligation or liability, express or implied, excepting those in § 15-3-520. § 15-3-520(b): twenty years for sealed instruments, except a sealed contract for sale of goods follows § 36-2-725. Editor's note: the period was reduced from six to three years in 1988.

title: Contract provision shortening the statutory period (Title 15, Chapter 3)
date_or_version: Current unannotated Code as shown on page
legal_subject: Contract clauses that shorten the time to sue
verification_status: Verified: page text read directly on scstatehouse.gov
what_it_says_and_notes: A contract clause (verbal or written) saying a party is barred from suing unless suit is brought in less time than the statute of limitations does not bar the action if it is brought within the statutory period. PRODUCT USE: a rule your analyzer can flag. Clauses that try to shorten the time to sue should be marked as likely ineffective under SC law, with this section as the source.

title: Commercial Code: Sales (UCC Article 2), Title 36, Chapter 2
date_or_version: Current unannotated Code as shown on page (Copyright notice 2026)
legal_subject: Contracts for the sale of goods: writing requirement, modification, unconscionability, warranty disclaimers, excuse, limiting remedies and damages
verification_status: Verified: page text read directly on scstatehouse.gov (sections 36-2-101 through 36-2-723 read)
what_it_says_and_notes: § 36-2-102: applies to transactions in goods. § 36-2-201: writing required for goods of $500 or more, with exceptions. § 36-2-209: modification needs no consideration; no-oral-modification clauses are enforceable with limits. § 36-2-302: court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable contract or clause. § 36-2-316: warranty disclaimers must mention merchantability and be conspicuous. § 36-2-718: liquidated damages must be reasonable or are void as a penalty. § 36-2-719: remedies may be limited; consequential damages may be limited unless unconscionable. Applies to GOODS, not services.

title: Statute of limitations in contracts for sale
legal_subject: Time limit to sue on a sales-of-goods contract
verification_status: Verified: full section text read on Justia (secondary host). The official scstatehouse.gov chapter page (row 4) contains the same section, which my read of it stopped short of (it ended at § 36-2-724)
what_it_says_and_notes: § 36-2-725(1): six years after the cause of action accrues for breach of any contract for sale. (2): warranty claims accrue when the breach is or should have been discovered. Resolves the conflict in secondary sources (some said four years): the answer is six years, confirmed by the Supreme Court in row 6. Compare the three-year general rule in row 2.

title: Myrtle Beach Lumber Co. v. Willoughby
legal_subject: Contract interpretation: ambiguity construed against the drafter

what_it_says_and_notes: Supplier's form agreement was ambiguous; the court affirmed judgment for the owners and stated that an ambiguity in a written contract is construed most strongly against the drafters, quoting 17A C.J.S. Contracts § 324. Subsequent-history check not completed.

title: Williams v. Teran, Inc.
legal_subject: Contract interpretation: intent of the parties; ambiguity resolved against the party whose business it was to speak without ambiguity
authority_type: Case (binding precedent, if still good law)
verification_status: Verified: full opinion read on Hall Approved (secondary host built from CourtListener data); 32 later published cases cite it, including S.C. Court of Appeals decisions as recent as 2024
what_it_says_and_notes: Concededly ambiguous guaranty; court gives effect to the parties' intent and may consider the circumstances of execution; where a contract can be read more than one way, doubt is resolved against the party whose business it was to speak without ambiguity (guarantors who authored the letter).
